open.speaker: tn_landlady
lines: tn_landlady
Breakfast is eight, sharp, and the front door's bolted at eleven, and I don't care what the Americans do at home. Mrs Bannister. You're in 4 and 5.
tn_landlady
Yes, 4. The Mallory girl's. I thought you'd want it. Most people who come about 1973 want it, though they don't say so till they've seen the wallpaper.
ruth
She's put us in the child's room on purpose, dear. That's either a kindness or an experiment.

passives.line: The register's open on the hall table. Not at this week. At a page whose corner's gone soft as cloth from being turned to.
She says 'the Mallory girl'. Fay is twenty-seven and works in the chemist a hundred yards away. In this house she's still seven.

options.text: Room 4 is fine, Mrs Bannister. Thank you for thinking of it.
We'll want the register, the room, and breakfast when we say.
The wallpaper's held up well. Has the rest of the story?

welcome.speaker: tn_landlady
lines: tn_landlady
Well. You've manners, which is more than the man from the Sunday paper had in '83. He wanted the room too, and he smoked in it.
tn_landlady
There's a kettle. There's a tide table on the back of the door, which you'll want more than the kettle.

rules.speaker: tn_landlady
lines: tn_landlady
You'll want a lot of things. You'll get breakfast at eight. I've had the Rudds, the Mallorys and the Sunday papers, and none of them told me when.
miriam
We're guests in a house that's seen worse guests than us and liked them less. Pull it in.

hub.speaker: tn_landlady
lines: tn_landlady
Forty years keeping this house. Full board, half board, and a week in May 1973 I've had to do over in my head every night since. Ask, then, I've the beds to turn.
hub.prompt: Mrs Bannister keeps one hand flat on the register.

options.text: You put us in Room 4 on purpose. What do you want us to find in it?

fail.line: I put you in it because it's got two singles. Don't read into my beds.

options.text: That page is soft at the corner. You read it every night. Read it to us once.
Her mother took the crayons on the Thursday. You cleared the breakfast table on the Wednesday. You kept one.
Stray Alsatian, eighty-one degrees. Both children at your table. Did the paper ask you?
That's all for now, Mrs Bannister.

static.line: Room 3's key is on the hook with no number on it. She's never let it since. Ask her why the number's gone.

room4.speaker: tn_landlady
lines: tn_landlady
...Nobody sleeps the night through in it. Twenty-one years of guests, and every one of them down at breakfast saying the room's lovely but did I hear the pier last night.
tn_landlady
There's no pier on that side. There's the Levels. If you hear it, you'll know what she heard, and you can tell me, because I've never dared sleep in it myself.
elijah
She's used us as a thermometer. I don't mind. Somebody has to go in and read it.

page.speaker: tn_landlady
lines: tn_landlady
...Saturday the 26th. Rudd, Mr and Mrs and Colin, Room 2. Mallory, Mr and Mrs and Fay, Room 4. Tappin, R., Sunnyside, Room 3, paid in advance, cash.
tn_landlady
Cash out of a Sunnyside wage packet, brown, with the camp's stamp on it. I noticed because they never paid their lot till the Friday.
tn_landlady
He'd been paid on a Saturday. Before he'd done a day.
miriam
Paid before he'd worked. That's not wages. That's a fee. Somebody at that camp bought a week of him.

page_fail.speaker: tn_landlady
lines: tn_landlady
I keep the register. I don't perform it. If you want 1973 read aloud, Miss Jolliffe at the library has the paper on the machine and she's paid to.
teddy
Sent to the library. Politely. She's not refused, she's rationed.

drawing.speaker: tn_landlady
lines: tn_landlady
...I kept one. Off the tablecloth, Wednesday, she'd done it in the jam. I copied it onto a card before I washed the cloth. I don't know why. I've never known why.
tn_landlady
It's dials. A row of them, and every needle pointing the same way, and a tall thing at the end with no face. I've got it in the dresser drawer and I've never shown Fay.
tn_landlady
Don't tell her I've got it. If she wants it, she can ask me. She's never asked me anything.
ruth
Twenty-one years in a dresser drawer. She's been keeping it for the child, dear, and the child grew up a hundred yards away and never came.

drawing_fail.speaker: tn_landlady
lines: tn_landlady
I cleared a table. I've cleared ten thousand tables. Breakfast is at eight and I'll thank you not to be in my kitchen before it.
miriam
That was a guess dressed as a fact. She caught it. Fay might know. Fay's the one who drew it.

paper.speaker: tn_landlady
lines: tn_landlady
Nobody asked me. A policeman came, and he wrote down 'Alsatian' while I was still talking, and the paper took what he wrote. I'd have said. Nobody asked.
tn_landlady
I'd have said two children came in off that marsh and neither of them had been near a dog, because I'd have smelt it on them. I smell everything in this house.
teddy
The one witness who had both kids at her table, and the only question she ever got was from us. Twenty-one years late.
